alt: Crime and Deviance (3.3.1) and Theory and Methods (3.3.2) combine into Paper 3, a single examination. The four content areas are social order and control, the social distribution of crime, crime at a global and institutional scale, and responses to crime.
caption: Paper 3 examines Crime and Deviance together with Theory and Methods.

alt: An explanation of crime links to two core themes: socialisation, culture and identity (for example, subcultural values and how group norms are learned) and social differentiation, power and stratification (for example, whose behaviour is defined as criminal).
caption: A strong answer connects each theory of crime to one or both core themes.

alt: A grid comparing consensus, conflict and interactionist or labelling explanations. Each column shows what crime is in that view and how it would explain class differences in crime.
caption: Consensus, conflict and labelling give three different answers to why crime varies by class.

alt: The question of how harmful behaviour is defined and by whom applies to individual offenders, to corporations through green crime, and to states through state crime and human rights violations.
caption: Green crime and state crime extend the same theoretical debate beyond the individual offender.

alt: A chain from media representation of crime to public perception of who commits crime, to policing priorities, to the official statistics that are recorded.
caption: Media images of crime can feed through perception and policing into the statistics.

alt: Official statistics capture only reported and recorded crime and are shaped by policing practices, while self-report and victim studies capture crime that may never appear in official records.
caption: Different data sources give different pictures of the social distribution of crime.
